_comment_: Master parcel registry. Atlas-grounded facts about cortical regions, independent of any paper or view. View configs reference parcels here by stable ID. When atlas data replaces hand-tuned centroids, only centroid/radius/provenance change. The `note` field is a function-focused, plain-language description used by the glossary tooltip — describes what the region does or why it matters, not where it is.

lang.LanA-IFGorb-L.label: IFG-orbital
lang.LanA-IFGorb-L.note: Orbital portion of Broca's territory. Implicated in higher-level semantic and pragmatic processing — meaning, intent, and discourse-level context in language.

lang.LanB-IFG-L.label: IFG (Broca's)
lang.LanB-IFG-L.note: Classic Broca's area. Associated with speech production and syntactic processing; damage produces non-fluent aphasia — comprehension preserved, but speech becomes laboured and halting.

lang.LanC-MFG-L.label: MFG
lang.LanC-MFG-L.note: Middle frontal portion of the language network. Recruited for verbal working memory during sentence processing — holding words in mind while structure is built.

lang.LanD-AntTemp-L.label: Anterior temporal
lang.LanD-AntTemp-L.note: Semantic hub. Combines word meanings into concepts and stores knowledge about objects, people, and events; degrades selectively in semantic dementia, where word meaning is lost while grammar is preserved.

lang.LanE-PostTemp-L.label: Posterior temporal
lang.LanE-PostTemp-L.note: Wernicke's area. Maps spoken and written word forms to meaning; damage produces fluent but uncomprehended speech — words flow, but content is lost.

tom.TPJ-L.label: TPJ-L
tom.TPJ-L.layCue: left side, where the temporal and parietal lobes meet
tom.TPJ-L.note: Theory-of-mind hub. Engages when reasoning about other people's beliefs, intentions, and knowledge states; left TPJ is recruited especially during sustained social-narrative comprehension.

tom.TPJ-R.label: TPJ-R
tom.TPJ-R.note: Right-hemisphere theory-of-mind hub. Particularly responsive to false-belief reasoning — updating mental models when someone else's perspective differs from your own.

tom.MTG-L.label: MTG-L
tom.MTG-L.note: Middle temporal gyrus, left. Part of the social-narrative network; tracks character mental states and integrates meaning across narrative.

tom.MTG-R.label: MTG-R
tom.MTG-R.note: Right MTG within the bilateral mentalising network. Engaged when modelling others' minds, especially during socially-rich narrative.

yeo.DMN-dmPFC.label: dmPFC
yeo.DMN-dmPFC.note: Dorsomedial prefrontal cortex. Self-referential thought and mentalising — active when you think about your own traits, autobiographical memories, or the inner life of close others.

yeo.DMN-Precuneus.label: Precuneus
yeo.DMN-Precuneus.layCue: middle of the inside surface, toward the back
yeo.DMN-Precuneus.note: Central node of the default mode network. Engaged during mind-wandering, autobiographical memory retrieval, and self-referential thought; one of the most metabolically-active regions during rest.

yeo.DMN-PCC.label: PCC
yeo.DMN-PCC.note: Posterior cingulate cortex. Quiet during external task focus and intensely active during rest, daydreaming, and inward attention — a barometer for whether the brain is turned in or out.

dk.lh-frontal-coarse.label: L frontal (coarse)
dk.lh-frontal-coarse.note: Coarse left-frontal territory used by the original Four Modes view. Covers the broad task-positive frontal cortex — executive control regions in left hemisphere.

dk.lh-parietal-coarse.label: L parietal (coarse)
dk.lh-parietal-coarse.note: Coarse left-parietal territory. Spatial attention and goal-directed control; supports keeping a task in mind while you work on it.

dk.rh-frontal-coarse.label: R frontal (coarse)
dk.rh-frontal-coarse.note: Coarse right-frontal territory. Probabilistic and inductive reasoning — weighing evidence under uncertainty rather than chaining formal rules.

dk.rh-parietal-coarse.label: R parietal (coarse)
dk.rh-parietal-coarse.note: Coarse right-parietal territory. Numerosity and magnitude estimation — comparing quantities, gauging how-likely or how-much rather than computing exact values.

_comment_triple_network_: Triple Network parcels (Phase B). Yeo 2011 7-network atlas regions for CEN; existing yeo.DMN-* + new yeo7.DMN.AG-* angular gyrus parcels for DMN; Seeley 2007 anterior insula + ACC for SN.

yeo7.CEN.dlPFC-L.label: L dlPFC (CEN)
yeo7.CEN.dlPFC-L.layCue: upper front of your forehead, left side
yeo7.CEN.dlPFC-L.note: Left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. The cognitive-control workhorse: holds task goals in working memory, plans action, and suppresses distraction.

yeo7.CEN.dlPFC-R.label: R dlPFC (CEN)
yeo7.CEN.dlPFC-R.layCue: upper front of your forehead, right side
yeo7.CEN.dlPFC-R.note: Right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Mirrors the left in executive control with somewhat greater involvement in inhibition and rule maintenance.

yeo7.CEN.IPL-L.label: L IPL (CEN)
yeo7.CEN.IPL-L.note: Left inferior parietal lobule, control portion. Attentional control and integration of task-relevant signals; works with dlPFC to keep behaviour goal-directed.

yeo7.CEN.IPL-R.label: R IPL (CEN)
yeo7.CEN.IPL-R.note: Right inferior parietal lobule. Sustained attention and goal-directed orientation; important for maintaining vigilance over time.

yeo7.DMN.AG-L.label: L Angular Gyrus (DMN)
yeo7.DMN.AG-L.note: Left angular gyrus, default-mode portion. Semantic integration — combining word meanings, memory, and context to form richer conceptual structures.

yeo7.DMN.AG-R.label: R Angular Gyrus (DMN)
yeo7.DMN.AG-R.note: Right angular gyrus. Bilateral DMN node; supports integrating context and abstract relationships during sustained narrative or rest.

seeley.SN.AI-L.label: L Anterior Insula
seeley.SN.AI-L.layCue: hidden inside the lateral fissure, on the left
seeley.SN.AI-L.note: Left anterior insula. Detects what matters in the moment — salience signals — and gates the switch between executive control (CEN) and default-mode states.

seeley.SN.AI-R.label: R Anterior Insula
seeley.SN.AI-R.layCue: hidden inside the lateral fissure, on the right
seeley.SN.AI-R.note: Right anterior insula. Especially attuned to interoceptive (body-state) signals and emotional salience — what's important in the world right now.

seeley.SN.ACC.label: ACC
seeley.SN.ACC.note: Dorsal anterior cingulate cortex. Conflict monitoring, error detection, and effort allocation; works tightly with the anterior insula in salience-based switching.

_comment_vwfa_: VWFA parcel (Phase C). Cohen 2002 reports the Visual Word Form Area as a focal patch on the left mid-fusiform gyrus, approx MNI (-43, -54, -12). Small radius reflects its reported focal extent (~5mm cluster).

cohen2002.VWFA.label: VWFA
cohen2002.VWFA.layCue: bottom of the brain, left side, where vision meets meaning
cohen2002.VWFA.note: Visual Word Form Area. Activates rapidly and selectively for written words across fonts and presentation; develops only with literacy — readers and non-readers show striking differences in this region.

_comment_cortical_networks_: Parcels for the `cortical-networks` view (8 systems: language, ToM, prosody, face/gesture, motor, salience, episodic memory, emotion). Unlike every parcel above, these centroids are NOT hand-tuned — each is the vertex centroid of an explicitly-declared subset of fsaverage Desikan-Killiany pial labels, computed by scripts/derive-parcel-centroids.mjs. The `derivation` field records the exact label set and axis slice. Re-run that script after any edit; test/brain-viz/parcel-centroid-sync.test.js fails if these numbers drift from what it produces. IDs are anatomy-first (`cn.`) rather than network-prefixed because several regions belong to more than one network — one shared parcel is what makes the renderer blend the two network colors.
_comment_cortical_networks_authorship_: AUTHORSHIP: every `note` and `layCue` string in this section was drafted by Claude, not written by Irwin. They are factual region descriptions, not authored prose, but they have not been reviewed. Treat as provisional copy pending review.
_comment_cortical_networks_mni_: The `mniPeak` values are group-level partition peaks transcribed from Fedorenko et al. 2010, Table 1 (J Neurophysiol 104:1177-1194, p. 1184). They are reference metadata for the glossary and do NOT drive placement: the pial OBJs are in FreeSurfer tkrRAS, which differs from MNI by an offset that is not a clean affine, so projecting these coordinates would misplace regions by a centimetre or more.

cn.IFGorb-L.label: IFG-orbital (L)
cn.IFGorb-L.layCue: left side, above and behind the outer corner of your eye
cn.IFGorb-L.note: Orbital part of the inferior frontal gyrus, the lowest of the three frontal language regions. Recruited for semantic and pragmatic aspects of comprehension — meaning and intent rather than word order.

cn.IFG-L.label: IFG (L)
cn.IFG-L.layCue: left side, just behind your temple
cn.IFG-L.note: Left inferior frontal gyrus, the frontal end of the language network. Responds far more to sentences than to strings of pronounceable nonwords, which is the contrast the whole network is defined by. Do not read this as Broca's area: Fedorenko argues that Broca's is a speech area supporting motor planning for articulation, sitting next to this one rather than being it. The speech-motor patch is drawn separately in the motor network.

cn.MFG-L.label: MFG (L)
cn.MFG-L.layCue: left side of your forehead, upper half
cn.MFG-L.note: Middle frontal gyrus. The most dorsal of the frontal language regions, and the one that sits closest to domain-general executive cortex — one reason the language and multiple-demand networks are easy to confuse in group-averaged data.

cn.AntTemp-L.label: Anterior temporal (L)
cn.AntTemp-L.layCue: left side, in front of and below your ear
cn.AntTemp-L.note: Anterior temporal lobe. Combines word meanings into larger concepts; degrades selectively in semantic dementia, where grammar survives but word meaning drains away.

cn.MidPostTemp-L.label: Mid-posterior temporal (L)
cn.MidPostTemp-L.layCue: left side, directly below your ear
cn.MidPostTemp-L.note: Mid-posterior temporal cortex. The region where individual subjects' language activation overlaps most reliably — Fedorenko 2010 puts the densest overlap hotspots within a few millimetres of here.

cn.PostTemp-L.label: Posterior temporal (L)
cn.PostTemp-L.layCue: left side, behind your ear (Wernicke's territory)
cn.PostTemp-L.note: Posterior temporal cortex, overlapping classical Wernicke's area. Maps word forms onto meaning; damage produces speech that stays fluent while comprehension collapses.

cn.AngG-L.label: Angular gyrus (L)
cn.AngG-L.layCue: left side, high and toward the back
cn.AngG-L.note: Left angular gyrus. The least typical member of the language network: in Paunov 2019's clustering it repeatedly grouped with the Theory of Mind regions instead of with the rest of the language system.

cn.IFG-R.label: IFG (R)
cn.IFG-R.layCue: right side, just behind your temple
cn.IFG-R.mniPeakSource: Sammler 2015 Table 1, R IFG pars opercularis
cn.IFG-R.note: Right inferior frontal gyrus, the mirror of the left language network's frontal node. Mineroff 2018 defines the right language regions by transposing the left masks. It also sits at the frontal end of the prosody stream, which is why this parcel belongs to two networks here.

cn.PostTemp-R.label: Posterior temporal (R)
cn.PostTemp-R.note: Right posterior temporal cortex. Responds to language but far more weakly than its left counterpart; Mineroff 2018 found left and right language regions cluster as separate branches rather than one bilateral system.

cn.TPJ-L.label: TPJ (L)
cn.TPJ-L.layCue: left side, where the temporal and parietal lobes meet
cn.TPJ-L.note: Left temporoparietal junction. Responds when you reason about what someone else believes rather than what is actually the case. That effect is equally strong on both sides; what sets the left apart in Saxe & Kanwisher 2003 is that it answered only to mental states described in words, where the right also picked up photographs of people.

cn.TPJ-R.label: TPJ (R)
cn.TPJ-R.layCue: right side, where the temporal and parietal lobes meet
cn.TPJ-R.note: Right temporoparietal junction. Belief reasoning engages it about as strongly as the left — Saxe & Kanwisher 2003 report the two did not differ on that contrast — and if anything the right is the broader of the pair, responding to pictures of people as well as to descriptions of them. Paunov 2019 found it among the ToM regions most strongly synchronised with the language network during story listening.

cn.dMPFC-L.label: dMPFC (L)
cn.dMPFC-L.layCue: behind your forehead, on the inner surface, left of midline
cn.dMPFC-L.note: Dorsomedial prefrontal cortex. Active when you think about other people's enduring traits and intentions rather than their momentary beliefs. Drawn here as a left-right pair because the underlying atlas splits the midline by hemisphere; the source that defines this region treats it as a single midline patch, so read the two spheres as one.

cn.dMPFC-R.label: dMPFC (R)
cn.dMPFC-R.layCue: behind your forehead, on the inner surface, right of midline
cn.dMPFC-R.note: Right dorsomedial prefrontal cortex. Mentalising node; part of the bilateral medial-frontal contribution to social reasoning.

cn.vMPFC.label: vMPFC
cn.vMPFC.layCue: behind and above your eyes, on the midline
cn.vMPFC.note: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Sits in both the mentalising network and the valuation circuitry — it is where judgements about other people and judgements about worth are hard to pull apart.

cn.PC-L.label: Precuneus / PCC (L)
cn.PC-L.layCue: on the inner surface, toward the back and top
cn.PC-L.note: Left precuneus and posterior cingulate. A hub shared by mentalising and episodic recall — both involve constructing a scene you are not currently perceiving.

cn.PC-R.label: Precuneus / PCC (R)
cn.PC-R.layCue: on the inner surface, toward the back and top
cn.PC-R.note: Right precuneus and posterior cingulate. Among the most metabolically active cortex at rest, and one of the first regions to quiet down when attention turns outward.

cn.HG-R.label: Heschl's gyrus (R)
cn.HG-R.layCue: buried in the fold above your right ear
cn.HG-R.note: Right primary auditory cortex — the first cortical stop for sound. Belin 2000 places the central of its three voice-selective clusters roughly at the level of the anterior extension of Heschl's gyrus, so voice-sensitive cortex begins close by without being auditory cortex itself. Fedorenko 2024 lists it among the areas engaged during speech perception but not selectively so: it responds to sound in general, and is sensitive only to the surface form of a linguistic signal, never to its meaning. Its bias toward slow spectral change is why speech melody is handled more on this side than the left.

cn.STG-R.label: STG (R)
cn.STG-R.layCue: right side, just above your ear
cn.STG-R.note: Right superior temporal gyrus. Tracks pitch contour, timing and voice quality — the parts of an utterance that carry who is speaking and how they mean it, rather than which words they used.

cn.STS-R.label: STS (R)
cn.STS-R.layCue: right side, in the long groove below your ear level
cn.STS-R.note: Right superior temporal sulcus. Voice-selective cortex: responds more to human vocalisations than to matched non-vocal sounds, including vocalisations with no words in them at all.

cn.PMC-R.label: Premotor (R)
cn.PMC-R.layCue: right side, high up, just in front of the motor strip
cn.PMC-R.note: Right premotor cortex, at what Sammler 2015 calls the larynx representation. The frontal end of the dorsal prosody stream. Inhibiting it with repetitive TMS made people measurably worse at telling a question from a statement by tone alone, which makes it one of the few nodes on this figure implicated causally rather than by correlation.

_comment_vwfa_: cn.VWFA-L and cn.FFA-L are both slices of lh.fusiform, and their proximity is the claim rather than a compromise. Dehaene 2014 reports that as literacy rises, responses to faces fall in the left hemisphere and rise in the right FFA — words and faces competing for the same cortical territory. Reich 2011 places the VWFA in the occipitotemporal sulcus, the lateral bank of the fusiform, so the spec adds a lateral x slice; derived that way it lands posterior, lateral and slightly superior to FFA-L, which is what the literature reports. Reich gives Talairach and Dehaene-Lambertz 2018 gives MNI for the same region; only the Talairach pair is stored, per the one-space-per-parcel rule.

cn.VWFA-L.label: VWFA (L)
cn.VWFA-L.layCue: underside of the brain, left side, toward the back
cn.VWFA-L.note: Visual word form area. The one piece of cortex that reading reliably takes over, in every writing system tested. It is not really visual: congenitally blind people reading Braille peak here too, within a couple of voxels of where sighted readers do, and it stays left-lateralised whichever hand they read with. Reich 2011 proposes calling it a metamodal word form area for that reason. How strongly it responds tracks how well a person reads, from illiterate to expert.

cn.FFA-L.label: FFA (L)
cn.FFA-L.layCue: underside of the brain, left side
cn.FFA-L.note: Left fusiform face area, the weaker of the pair. Kanwisher 1997 found a right fusiform response in every right-handed subject who showed the effect but a left one in only five of ten, at half the volume and lower significance. Face selectivity is right-dominant rather than right-exclusive.

cn.FFA-R.label: FFA (R)
cn.FFA-R.layCue: underside of the brain, right side
cn.FFA-R.note: Right fusiform face area. Across Kanwisher 1997's five specificity tests it responded between about three and six times more strongly to faces than to the comparison category — objects, houses, scrambled faces or hands — with the largest gap against houses. Damage here produces prosopagnosia: intact vision, intact language, no ability to recognise a face.

cn.pSTS-L.label: Posterior STS (L)
cn.pSTS-L.layCue: left side, in the groove toward the back of the temporal lobe
cn.pSTS-L.note: Left posterior superior temporal sulcus. Reads biological motion: the shape of a gesture, the direction of a gaze. It sits at the far back end of the same long fold whose front end handles language, about five centimetres away rather than adjacent. The overlap language actually has along this sulcus is with mental-state reasoning, not with motion.

cn.pSTS-R.label: Posterior STS (R)
cn.pSTS-R.layCue: right side, in the groove toward the back of the temporal lobe
cn.pSTS-R.note: Right posterior superior temporal sulcus. Deen 2015 mapped several overlapping response zones along this fold, ordered back to front: mental-state reasoning, then biological motion, then faces, then voices, then language at the front. Neighbouring zones share between a fifth and a half of their voxels. The same ordering appears on both sides. Whether that overlap means one population doing several jobs, or separate populations woven together, the paper leaves open.

cn.OFA-R.label: Occipital face area (R)
cn.OFA-R.layCue: back of the head, right side
cn.OFA-R.note: Right occipital face area. An earlier stage than the fusiform face area — handles parts of a face (an eye, a mouth) before the fusiform assembles them into a recognisable person.

cn.M1-L.label: M1 — primary motor (L)
cn.M1-L.layCue: left side, along the ridge running over the top of your head
cn.M1-L.note: Left primary motor cortex. Sends movement commands to the right side of the body, laid out as an ordered map from toes at the midline down to the face at the bottom.

cn.M1-R.label: M1 — primary motor (R)
cn.M1-R.layCue: right side, along the ridge over the top of your head
cn.M1-R.note: Right primary motor cortex, controlling the left side of the body. Pritchett 2018 found watching and imitating actions leaves the language network unmoved — motor and language work stays separate.

cn.S1-L.label: S1 — somatosensory (L)
cn.S1-L.layCue: left side, just behind the motor ridge
cn.S1-L.note: Left primary somatosensory cortex. Receives touch and limb position from the right side of the body; pairs with M1 to close the loop between moving and feeling the movement.

cn.SMA.label: SMA
cn.SMA.layCue: top of the brain, on the midline, slightly forward
cn.SMA.note: Supplementary motor area. Sequences and initiates movement rather than executing it. Heavily involved in speech timing, which is why it shows up in speech studies that have nothing to do with meaning.

cn.artic-L.label: Articulatory motor (L)
cn.artic-L.layCue: left side, low on the motor strip, near your temple
cn.artic-L.note: The mouth-and-tongue portion of the left motor strip, adjacent to Broca's articulatory planning area. Fedorenko 2024 separates this speech-motor machinery from the language network proper: it plans and executes oro-facial movement, is engaged during but not selectively for speech, and responds to the surface form of an utterance rather than its meaning. Language needs it to get words out of the mouth; it is not part of the language network.

cn.AI-L.label: Anterior insula (L)
cn.AI-L.layCue: hidden deep inside the left temple fold
cn.AI-L.note: Left anterior insula. Flags what matters right now and helps hand control between inward and outward attention. Craig 2009 treats the anterior insula as the sensory half of a limbic pair with the anterior cingulate — it registers the state of the body, the cingulate acts on it. Left-sided activation is reported for pleasant music and for gastric fullness, which arrives on vagal afferents.

cn.AI-R.label: Anterior insula (R)
cn.AI-R.layCue: hidden deep inside the right temple fold
cn.AI-R.mniPeakSource: Seeley 2007, right orbital frontoinsula seed ROI
cn.AI-R.note: Right anterior insula. Reads the state of the body — heart rate, gut, breath — and turns it into the feeling that something is significant. Craig 2009 gathers the evidence for right dominance in interoception: heartbeat awareness, the subjective evaluation of heat pain, and attention to a painful stimulus all favour this side, and interoceptive information appears to integrate along a posterior-to-anterior gradient toward it.

cn.dACC.label: dACC
cn.dACC.layCue: midline, wrapped over the front of the corpus callosum
cn.dACC.mniPeakSource: Seeley 2007, dACC cluster tracking prescan anxiety
cn.dACC.note: Dorsal anterior cingulate. Detects conflict and errors and decides how much effort a task is worth. Works as a pair with the anterior insula.

cn.Hipp-L.label: Hippocampus (L)
cn.Hipp-L.layCue: deep inside, level with your ears
cn.Hipp-L.derivation: lh.parahippocampal + offset [0.045, 0.085, 0.03] (approximate — no DK surface label)
cn.Hipp-L.note: Left hippocampus. Binds the pieces of an experience into a retrievable episode. Position here is approximate: the hippocampus is subcortical and has no surface label in the Desikan-Killiany parcellation, so it is placed relative to the parahippocampal gyrus.

cn.Hipp-R.label: Hippocampus (R)
cn.Hipp-R.layCue: deep inside, level with your ears
cn.Hipp-R.derivation: rh.parahippocampal + offset [-0.045, 0.085, 0.03] (approximate — no DK surface label)
cn.Hipp-R.note: Right hippocampus, with a stronger bias toward spatial and scene memory than the left. Approximate placement — subcortical, so anchored to the parahippocampal gyrus rather than derived from its own mesh.

cn.PHC-L.label: Parahippocampal (L)
cn.PHC-L.layCue: underside of the brain, toward the middle
cn.PHC-L.note: Left parahippocampal cortex. Feeds context — the where and the setting — into the hippocampus during encoding and retrieval.

cn.PHC-R.label: Parahippocampal (R)
cn.PHC-R.layCue: underside of the brain, toward the middle
cn.PHC-R.note: Right parahippocampal cortex, containing the place area that responds to scenes and spatial layouts far more than to objects or faces.

cn.EntC-L.label: Entorhinal (L)
cn.EntC-L.layCue: underside, well forward, near the tip of the temporal lobe
cn.EntC-L.note: Left entorhinal cortex. The gateway into the hippocampus — nearly everything that becomes an episodic memory passes through here first, and it is among the earliest sites of Alzheimer's pathology.

cn.EntC-R.label: Entorhinal (R)
cn.EntC-R.layCue: underside, well forward, near the tip of the temporal lobe
cn.EntC-R.note: Right entorhinal cortex. Carries the grid-cell machinery that maps space, and passes it into the hippocampus alongside the rest of an episode.

cn.RSC.label: Retrosplenial
cn.RSC.layCue: midline, low and toward the back
cn.RSC.note: Retrosplenial cortex. Translates between a view from where you are standing and a map-like sense of where things are — central to both navigation and remembering a place you are not in.

_comment_unreferenced_2026_08_05_: cn.EntC-L, cn.EntC-R and cn.sgACC are currently referenced by NO view. Entorhinal cortex was removed from the episodic network because Rugg & Vilberg tie it to familiarity rather than recollection, and neither it nor precuneus appears in that network in Rugg & Vilberg or Andrews-Hanna. Subgenual ACC lost its home when the emotion network was dropped. They are kept in the registry because the geometry is derived and correct — only the grouping was unsupported. Re-reference them when a source justifies it.
_comment_ofa_unreferenced_: cn.OFA-R is referenced by no view as of 2026-08-05. It was in the face network sourced to Kanwisher 1997, but that paper never mentions an occipital face area — the OFA-as-early-stage model comes from later work (Gauthier 2000, Pitcher/Duchaine). Re-reference it when a source that actually studies OFA is on disk.

cn.mMPFC.label: Middle MPFC
cn.mMPFC.layCue: behind the middle of your forehead, halfway up
cn.mMPFC.note: Middle band of medial prefrontal cortex. Dufour 2013 divides this stretch of the midline into three by height — dorsal, middle and ventral — and treats all three as mental-state regions. The middle band is the least reliably found of the three: it showed up in 64% of the 493 people scanned, against 94% for the right temporoparietal junction.

cn.aSTS-R.label: Anterior STS (R)
cn.aSTS-R.layCue: right side, in the groove below and in front of your ear
cn.aSTS-R.mniPeakSource: Saxe & Kanwisher 2003, right anterior STS (false belief > false photograph)
cn.aSTS-R.note: Right anterior superior temporal sulcus. Turned up as a mental-state region in both experiments of Saxe & Kanwisher 2003 and again in Dufour 2013's seven-region set, which is why it belongs here. It sits well forward of the patch on the same sulcus that reads bodies in motion.

_comment_music_: Music-selective parcels. Norman-Haignere 2015 found the music component in planum polare bilaterally and in left planum temporale. Desikan-Killiany has no label for either planum — both are folded into `superiortemporal` — so these are recovered with a superior slice (the supratemporal plane) plus a medial slice, which is also what keeps them clear of the language and prosody parcels on the lateral surface of the same gyrus. Left planum polare needed the tightest superior slice to clear cn.AntTemp-L.

cn.PP-L.label: Planum polare (L)
cn.PP-L.layCue: on the upper shelf of the temporal lobe, in front of the hearing area
cn.PP-L.note: Left planum polare, on the flat upper surface of the temporal lobe just in front of primary auditory cortex. Part of the cortex that responds to music more than to any other kind of sound, including speech and environmental noise.

cn.PP-R.label: Planum polare (R)
cn.PP-R.layCue: on the upper shelf of the temporal lobe, in front of the hearing area
cn.PP-R.note: Right planum polare. Music selectivity here is roughly as strong as on the left; Norman-Haignere 2015 found only a non-significant trend toward the left hemisphere, so this is one of the more even-handed systems on the figure.

cn.PT-L.label: Planum temporale (L)
cn.PT-L.layCue: on the upper shelf of the temporal lobe, behind the hearing area
cn.PT-L.note: Left planum temporale, the flat surface behind primary auditory cortex. The second site where Norman-Haignere 2015 found music selectivity. This patch is better known for speech and sound-sequence work, which is part of why music selectivity took a decomposition method to see at all.

_comment_md_network_: Multiple Demand parcels. Mineroff 2018 defines MD from Tzourio-Mazoyer AAL masks (IFGop, MFG, MFGorb, PrecG, Insula, SMA, InfPar, SupPar, AntCing per hemisphere); only the three pairs below get their own parcel, plus shares of cn.SMA and cn.dACC. MD's opercular IFG, precentral and insular nodes are deliberately omitted: derived from DK they land inside labels already claimed by the language, motor and salience networks (MD IFGop falls 0.07 from cn.IFG-L, well inside both radii). The MD/language dissociation is functional and spatially interleaved at a finer scale than any DK-derived figure can resolve — which is why group-averaged data conflates the two in the first place.

cn.MD-MFG-L.label: MFG (MD, L)
cn.MD-MFG-L.layCue: left forehead, high and well forward
cn.MD-MFG-L.note: Dorsal middle frontal gyrus, multiple-demand portion. Sits above and in front of the language network's MFG without overlapping it — the clearest place on this figure to see two networks as neighbours rather than one system. Recruited by hard tasks of almost any kind.

cn.MD-MFG-R.label: MFG (MD, R)
cn.MD-MFG-R.layCue: right forehead, high and well forward
cn.MD-MFG-R.note: Right dorsal middle frontal gyrus. The multiple-demand system is strongly bilateral, which is one of the things that most distinguishes it from the left-lateralised language network.

cn.MD-SupPar-L.label: Superior parietal (MD, L)
cn.MD-SupPar-L.layCue: top of the head, toward the back, left of midline
cn.MD-SupPar-L.note: Left superior parietal lobule. Engaged by spatial working memory, arithmetic and novel problem solving; damage across the multiple-demand system tracks loss of fluid intelligence.

cn.MD-SupPar-R.label: Superior parietal (MD, R)
cn.MD-SupPar-R.layCue: top of the head, toward the back, right of midline
cn.MD-SupPar-R.note: Right superior parietal lobule. Part of the bilateral parietal half of the multiple-demand system.

cn.MD-InfPar-L.label: Inferior parietal (MD, L)
cn.MD-InfPar-L.layCue: left side, high and toward the back
cn.MD-InfPar-L.note: Anterior inferior parietal cortex, multiple-demand portion. Sits just forward of the Theory of Mind network's temporoparietal junction and of the language network's angular gyrus — three networks within a couple of centimetres, none of them the same.

cn.MD-InfPar-R.label: Inferior parietal (MD, R)
cn.MD-InfPar-R.layCue: right side, high and toward the back
cn.MD-InfPar-R.note: Right anterior inferior parietal cortex. Responds to demanding tasks across domains — arithmetic, logic, working memory, comprehending computer code.

cn.Amyg-L.label: Amygdala (L)
cn.Amyg-L.layCue: deep inside, in front of the hippocampus
cn.Amyg-L.derivation: lh.entorhinal + offset [0.04, 0.105, 0.055] (approximate — no DK surface label)
cn.Amyg-L.note: Left amygdala. Tags events as threatening or significant and stamps that tag onto the memory being formed nearby. Approximate placement: subcortical, with no surface label in the Desikan-Killiany parcellation.

cn.Amyg-R.label: Amygdala (R)
cn.Amyg-R.layCue: deep inside, in front of the hippocampus
cn.Amyg-R.derivation: rh.entorhinal + offset [-0.04, 0.105, 0.055] (approximate — no DK surface label)
cn.Amyg-R.note: Right amygdala, faster than the left to respond to threat and more involved in automatic, unconscious appraisal. Approximate placement — anchored to entorhinal cortex rather than derived from its own mesh.

cn.sgACC.label: Subgenual ACC
cn.sgACC.layCue: midline, tucked under the front of the corpus callosum
cn.sgACC.note: Subgenual anterior cingulate. Overactive in depression and the target of deep brain stimulation for treatment-resistant cases — one of the few places where a mood state has a reliable address.
